t: Limit Occurrences in Sorted Array — Editorial
o: We must keep, for each distinct value in a sorted array, at most the first $k$ occurrences while preserving order. Since the array is sorted, all equal values are contiguous, so we can process each run of identical values as a block. In Example 1 with k=2: the run [1,1,1] contributes [1,1], [2,2] stays whole, and [3] stays — giving [1,1,2,2,3]. Example 2 has runs of length 1 ≤ k=1, so nothing is trimmed. Constraints (n ≤ 100) mean even an O(n²) solution passes easily, but a single-pass two-pointer solution is natural and optimal.
k: Sortedness means equal elements form contiguous runs, so one pass suffices.
A write pointer lets us build the answer in-place with O(1) extra space.
For each element, keep it only if fewer than k copies have already been written for that value.

a.i: Scan the sorted array and group equal values into contiguous runs. For each run, copy min(run length, k) occurrences into the result. This directly mirrors the problem statement and is easy to reason about, though it uses extra output bookkeeping via a counter reset per run.
s: Initialize an empty result list and i = 0.
While i < n, find j such that nums[i..j-1] is a maximal run of equal values.
Append min(j - i, k) copies of nums[i] to the result.
a.t: O(n) — each element is visited once by the outer scan plus once by run detection.
a.sp: O(n) for the output list (O(1) auxiliary beyond the output).

a.n: Approach 2: Two Pointers / In-place Write Pointer (Optimal)
a.i: Use a read pointer scanning every element and a write pointer marking where the next kept element goes. Keep a running count of how many times the current value has been written; since the array is sorted, the previous written element tells us when the value changes. An element is kept only if its written count so far is below k. This compacts the result into the front of the same array using O(1) extra space.
s: For each index r from 0 to n-1: if write > 0 and nums[write-1] == nums[r], increment count; else reset count = 1.
If count <= k, set nums[write++] = nums[r].
Return the first write elements of nums.
a.t: O(n) — single pass over the array with constant work per element.
a.sp: O(1) auxiliary — the result is compacted in-place; returned slices/copies don't count per the follow-up note.

w: In an interview, mention Approach 1 briefly to show clarity, then implement Approach 2 to demonstrate the O(1)-space two-pointer technique — it directly answers the follow-up. Pitfalls: forgetting to reset the count when the value changes (compare against nums[write-1], not nums[r-1], because overwritten positions shift), handling k ≥ run length correctly (keep everything), and n = 1. Edge cases: all elements identical, k = 1 (deduplication-like behavior). Likely follow-ups: solve without comparing neighbors using a hash map of counts (works even unsorted but costs O(n) space), or generalize to 'keep first k after sorting' variants.
